title: Showcase: three rounds against a parent
summary: A live three-round debate against a parent on whether a machine can surprise its own builder, argued hours after the flipped course, then the teach-someone-younger quest with the rhyme walk.
materials: a parent with fifteen minutes and opinions
this week's Sprout parent card, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: The rematch, live
steps.body:
This sprint you debated dangerous tools, trusting computers, and robot feelings. Today is the live one: three full rounds against a parent, no notes read aloud, and the freshest evidence you will ever hold, because hours ago you watched your own creature face terrain you never tuned it for.

The motion: a machine can surprise the person who built it. Think about the flipped course before you pick your side. Did the robot do anything you did not predict? And if it did, was that the machine surprising you, or just you not finishing your own thinking? Both readings are defensible, which is what makes this a real motion. Pick the side you actually lean toward; the parent takes the other. If you both lean the same way, the parent must steelman the far side, and you get to watch a grown-up argue against their own belief, which is a skill worth stealing.

The shape of the three rounds: round one, openings, one claim each with a reason and one example, and your best examples are sitting on today's course. Round two, rebuttal, and the steelman rule is strict: before you answer the parent's point, say it back so fairly that they nod. Round three, closings, one minute each, your single strongest example and nothing else.

If another family member is free, seat them as chair: they keep time and ask each side one hard question after round two. Voice rules as always: speak to the back wall, one pause on purpose, look at your opponent when you answer their point.

steps.title: Teach someone younger
steps.body:
A parent card is the short card in the app that a grown-up normally runs with Sprout. This week you run it, and this one is a giggle machine: the rhyme walk.

Read the card all the way through before you start, so you know where it is going. Then take a younger sibling, cousin or friend, or a parent playing the part, outside and play it straight: say the prompts, walk beside them, and listen hard.

One rule matters more than all the others today: made-up words count. If tree gets answered with zee or blee, that is not a mistake, that is the whole game, because they are playing with the sounds themselves. Laugh with them, never at them, and let them find every rhyme at their own speed, especially the slow ones.

Watch for one thing they do that surprises you: a rhyme you did not see coming, or a silly word that is better than any real one.
checklist: I read the card first, all the way through
They made the rhymes themselves, and I did not make any for them.
Made-up words were counted as wins, out loud
I noticed one thing they did that surprised me

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record round three of the debate: both closings, whole face in frame. Then keep the camera rolling for one honest sentence: which of your opponent's arguments was the strongest, and what would you say to it with another week to think?
